name: Puritans
info: The Puritans were English Protestants of the 16th and 17th centuries who sought to rid the Church of England of what they saw as Roman Catholic practices, came to power in the Civil War and settled New England.

facts.where: England and Wales, with ties to Scotland and the Continental Reformed churches; New England, above all the Massachusetts Bay Colony, Plymouth Colony, the Connecticut River colonies and Providence Plantations
facts.period: Elizabethan Settlement 1559; Millenary Petition 1603 and Hampton Court Conference 1604; Great Migration to New England 1629–1640; Westminster Assembly from 1643; Interregnum 1649–1660; Great Ejection 1662; Toleration Act 1689; Puritan hegemony in New England to 1728
facts.figures: Oliver Cromwell, an Independent and Lord Protector; Richard Baxter, ejected minister; William Bradshaw, who took the name Puritan for himself; John Winthrop, leading figure in founding the Massachusetts Bay Colony; Thomas Hooker, co-founder of the Connecticut Colony; Roger Williams, founder of Providence Plantations; Anne Hutchinson, banished from Massachusetts; Increase Mather and his son Cotton Mather, clergy of New England; John Milton and John Bunyan, writers
facts.outcome: political failure in England, where almost all Puritan clergy left the Church of England after 1660 and 1662 and many became nonconformists; a lasting legacy in the Westminster Standards, in Congregationalist and Presbyterian churches and in New England

t: The word Puritan began as a term of abuse; those so called spoke of themselves as "the godly", "saints", "professors" or "God's children".
Puritans were dissatisfied with the limited extent of the English Reformation and divided over church government between supporters of episcopal, presbyterian and congregational types.
Puritans came to power after the First English Civil War but never won the religious settlement they wanted; around 2,400 clergy left the Church of England in the Great Ejection of 1662.
dyk: Around 21,000 people crossed the Atlantic in the Puritan migration to New England, which ceased by 1641; their descendants in the United States number more than 16 million.
ev: The Elizabethan Religious Settlement establishes the Church of England as a Protestant church
James I holds the Hampton Court Conference, hears four Puritan leaders and largely sides with his bishops
Puritan emigration to New England begins and supports the founding of the Massachusetts Bay Colony
The Westminster Assembly is called and agrees the Westminster Confession of Faith
Parliament outlaws the celebration of Christmas, Easter and Whitsuntide
The first two of the four Quakers known as the Boston martyrs are hanged by the Puritans on 27 October
The Act of Uniformity leads around 2,400 Puritan clergy to leave the Church of England in the Great Ejection
The Toleration Act permits the licensing of Dissenting ministers and the building of chapels

sections.background:
The Elizabethan Religious Settlement of 1559 established the Church of England as a Protestant church and brought the English Reformation to a close. During the reign of Elizabeth I the church was widely considered a Reformed church, and Calvinists held the best bishoprics and deaneries. It nevertheless preserved characteristics of medieval Catholicism: cathedrals, church choirs, a formal liturgy in the Book of Common Prayer, traditional clerical vestments and episcopal polity.

Many English Protestants, especially the former Marian exiles who returned to work as clergy and bishops, considered the settlement only a first step. Their years of exile had exposed them to the practices of the Continental Reformed churches, and Geneva had hosted many of them. Puritans were dissatisfied with the limited extent of the Reformation and with the church's toleration of practices associated with the Catholic Church.

Puritan was originally a pejorative term. Thomas Fuller dated its first use to 1564, and Archbishop Matthew Parker used it and precisian in a sense similar to the modern stickler. Historians still debate a precise definition of Puritanism. Patrick Collinson argued that it was not a thing definable in itself but only one half of a stressful relationship.
sections.aims:
Puritans sought a church purged of what they regarded as Catholic remnants. They objected to the surplice and clerical cap, to bowing at the name of Jesus, to the sign of the cross in baptism, to wedding rings and to the organ. Many wanted set prayers replaced by improvised ones and the liturgy shortened to leave more time for the sermon, which was central to Puritan piety. They believed that all of their beliefs should rest on the Bible, which they considered divinely inspired.

Covenant theology was central. It held that God had promised Adam and Eve eternal life in return for perfect obedience, the covenant of works, which sinful humanity could not fulfil; Jesus's sacrifice made possible the covenant of grace for those God had chosen. Like other Calvinists, Puritans believed in double predestination. Conversion was described in phases, and Puritans came to regard a specific conversion experience as an essential mark of election.

On church government they divided. Episcopalians would keep bishops that supported reform, presbyterians wanted a system of elders on the model of the Church of Scotland, and Congregationalists or Independents held that each local church of visible saints was complete within itself. Some wanted a uniform reform of the established church; Separatists such as the Brownists wished to leave it.
sections.events:
In the 1570s the main dispute was over church government. Attempts to enact presbyterian reform through Parliament were blocked by the Queen, and John Field and James Lynch promoted presbyterianism through unofficial clerical conferences, a covert network discovered and dismantled during the Marprelate controversy of the 1580s. The Millenary Petition of 1603 was a Puritan manifesto, but at the Hampton Court Conference of 1604 James I largely sided with his bishops. Under Charles I Puritans became a political force, allied with opponents of the royal prerogative.

From 1629 to 1640 some Puritans left for New England, where the Massachusetts Bay Colony was founded. After the First English Civil War political power was held by various Puritan factions, and the trials and executions of William Laud and King Charles shaped British history. The Westminster Assembly, called in 1643, agreed the Westminster Confession of Faith, but its members were divided between reformed episcopacy, presbyterianism, congregationalism and Erastianism.

At the Restoration the Savoy Conference was called, and under the Act of Uniformity 1662 the Church of England was restored with only minor changes. About 2,400 Puritan clergy left it in the Great Ejection, a traditional estimate of Calamy; Richard Baxter estimated that 1,800 of them continued as ministers. The Clarendon Code was used against the Dissenters until the Toleration Act of 1689.
sections.people:
Oliver Cromwell was a Puritan and an independent Congregationalist Separatist who imposed his doctrines on the Westminster Assembly, and eventually became Lord Protector. His religious adviser was Philip Nye. William Bradshaw adopted the term Puritan for himself in the Jacobean period. Laurence Chaderton was one of four Puritan leaders heard at Hampton Court in 1604, and Vavasor Powell was a popular clergyman among the Fifth Monarchy Men.

In New England, John Winthrop is noted for his sermon "A Model of Christian Charity" and as a leading figure in founding the Massachusetts Bay Colony. William Bradford was governor of Plymouth Colony, John Endecott the first governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, and Thomas Hooker a co-founder of the Connecticut Colony. John Cotton and Richard Mather led the first generation, Increase Mather the second and Cotton Mather the third. Roger Williams set up Providence Plantations in 1636 with a formal separation of church and state.

Anne Hutchinson, the well educated daughter of a teacher, argued with the established theological orthodoxy and was forced to leave colonial New England with her followers. Anne Bradstreet was the first woman to have her works published in the British North American colonies. John Milton supported Cromwell and wrote Paradise Lost, and John Bunyan wrote The Pilgrim's Progress in 1678.
sections.outcomes:
In England the Puritan movement was riven over decades by emigration and inconsistent interpretations of Scripture. The Fifth Monarchy Men, a radical millenarian wing, agitated from the right wing of the movement, while sectarian groups such as the Ranters, Levellers and Quakers pulled from the left. The fragmentation created a collapse of the centre and sealed a political failure. England did not become the theocratic state that leading Puritans had called for as godly rule. The Church of England of the Interregnum was run along Presbyterian lines but never became a national Presbyterian church like Scotland's.

Where Puritans held power they enforced their moral standards. In 1647 Parliament outlawed Christmas, Easter and Whitsuntide, and pro-Christmas rioting broke out across England. English theatres were shut in the 1640s and 1650s. In Massachusetts, blasphemy was made punishable by death in 1636, and banishments, the whipping post and the branding iron were used to enforce conformity.

Intolerance of other faiths was shown in New England, where four Quakers, the Boston martyrs, were executed; Mary Dyer was hanged on Boston Common in 1660. In 1661 Charles II forbade Massachusetts to execute anyone for professing Quakerism. Salem's witch trials of 1692 ended with fourteen women and five men hanged, in proceedings that Puritans instigated, though they had lost political control of the colony.
sections.legacy:
The Westminster Assembly's formulation of Reformed theology would prove to be the movement's lasting legacy. Congregationalist churches are descended from the Puritans, and Puritan beliefs are enshrined in the Savoy Declaration, the confession of faith held by those churches. After 1662 the Dissenters formed the basis of later British Congregationalist, Baptist and Presbyterian traditions, and Nonconformist replaced Dissenter as the usual term from the middle of the 18th century. Puritanism's experiential piety was inherited by the evangelical Protestants of the 1700s.

Puritan political thought is credited with shaping political culture on both sides of the Atlantic. Robert Middlekauff argues that the comparatively secularised Radical Whig analysis fell on fertile American ground because Puritanism had left a suspicion of executive authority, while Zera Fink argued that Puritan political radicalism also owed a debt to classical republicanism. Robert K. Merton argued for a link between Puritanism and early experimental science, a thesis still debated, and Max Weber tied Calvinist self-denial to the rise of capitalism.

Puritan New England valued literacy: Boston Latin School was founded in 1635, Massachusetts required teaching of reading in 1642, and the college that became Harvard followed. The phrase "banned in Boston" was coined in the late 19th century. Peter Gay wrote that the Puritans' reputation for dour prudery was a misreading that went unquestioned in the nineteenth century.

summary: The Puritans were English Protestants who held that the Elizabethan church had not been fully reformed. They became a political force under Charles I and came to power after the First English Civil War, but won no settlement of their own in England. Many settled New England; their heirs include the Congregationalist churches.
references: Francis J. Bremer, Puritanism: A Very Short Introduction (Oxford University Press, 2009)
Patrick Collinson, The Birthpangs of Protestant England: Religious and Cultural Change in the Sixteenth and Seventeenth Centuries (Palgrave Macmillan, 1988)
Michael P. Winship, Hot Protestants: A History of Puritanism in England and America (Yale University Press, 2018)
notes: Dates: the article gives no start or end for the movement. I set start 1559 (the Elizabethan Settlement, with which its account of Elizabethan Puritanism opens) and end 1689 (the Toleration Act), both marked circa. The article also says Puritan hegemony in New England lasted to 1728 and that the term was rarely used after the turn of the 18th century. The editor may prefer other bounds.

Figures: the Great Ejection is 'around 2,400' by Calamy's traditional estimate and 'an estimated 1,800' continued as ministers according to Baxter; both attributed. New England witchcraft: the article says 'thirteen women and two men were executed between 1645 and 1663' and, for Salem, 'fourteen women and five men had been hanged'. I used only the Salem figure.

The article says the migration 'cease[d] by 1641' with around 21,000 persons; the event year 1629 is the start of the 1629 to 1640 period it names. It gives 'more than 16 million descendants', stated as the article's figure.

Left out: the sections on sex, homosexuality executions, family life, gender and censure, demonology in England (Hopkins), football and other recreation, alcohol, and Interregnum religious liberty, for length. The notable-Puritans list is brief and partly used in the people section.

The article says Cromwell 'imposed his doctrines upon' the Assembly; kept attributed to the article's account. The statement that the Quaker hanging 'marked the beginning of the end of the Puritan theocracy' is left out as a verdict.
